docs.title: rubrical
docs.text: A CLI to encourage (😅) people to update their dependencies!

docs.title: raison d'etre
docs.text:
Scenario: A team publishes an update to a new library that needs to be adopted.
            (New feature, breaking changes, security fixes, etc)
  Given your company has a microservice architecture
          (or >3 repositories to update across >2 teams )
  Then you go to each team and beg/bargin/plead for them to update their packages

You can (should!) use tools like renovate to automate dependency updates. But it's easy to lose track of updates especially with particularly technologies (hi JS/TS!) or busy teams.

rubrical breaks the cycle by putting a check inside your CI/CD pipelines. (Golden pipelines or shared workflows are highly recommended!) Now teams have a tool to automatically (automagically!) communicated when a dependency needs to be upgraded!

For more information, checkout the documentation!

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Set warning (notify users their dependency will be out of date soon) and block (exit with error code) levels.
  • Supports different languages (Python, Go, Node.js, and Jsonnet) and package manager formats (e.g. pip, poetry).
  • Post results to Github/GHE PRs.

docs.title: grade
docs.text:
A CLI to encourage (😅) people to update their dependencies!

Usage:

$ grade [OPTIONS]

Options:

  • --config PATH: Path to configuration [default: rubrical.yaml]
  • --target PATH: Path to configuration [default: /workspaces/rubrical]
  • --block / --no-block: Fail if blocks found. Overrides blocking_mode in the configuration. [default: (blocking_mode from configuration)]
  • --repository-name TEXT: Repository name for reporting purposes. [env var: RUBRICAL_REPOSITORY]
  • --pr-id INTEGER: PR ID for reporting purposes. [env var: RUBRICAL_PR_ID; default: 0]
  • --gh-access-token TEXT: Github access token for reporting. Presence will enable Github reporting. [env var: RUBRICAL_GH_TOKEN]
  • --gh-custom-url TEXT: Github Enterprise custom url. e.g. https://github.custom.dev [env var: RUBRICAL_GH_CUSTOM_URL]
  • --report-id TEXT: Keep a separate Github comment per report ID, e.g. one per service in a monorepo. [env var: RUBRICAL_REPORT_ID]
  • --debug / --no-debug: Enable debug messages [env var: RUBRICAL_DEBUG, RUBGRICAL_DEBUG; default: no-debug]
  • --help: Show this message and exit.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Rubrical uses a YAML/JSON/TOml file is used to configure checks for your application. By default, it will use the rubrical.yaml in your local directory. You can specify your own file with the --config flag.

version: 1
blocking_mode: true  # Optional, default true.  If false, blocked dependencies are reported but rubrical exits 0.
languages:  # Optional.  Grades the language versions your repository declares.
  - name: python  # One of python, go, nodejs.  Each language may only be listed once.
    block: v3.10.0  # If the lowest version allowed is less than this, error.
    warn: v3.12.0  # If the lowest version allowed is less than this, warn.
  - name: go
    block: v1.20.0
    warn: v1.22.0
  - name: nodejs
    block: v18.17.0
    warn: v20.0.0
package_managers:  # Optional.
  - name: jsonnet
    packages:
      - name: "xunleii/vector_jsonnet" # Name of the dependency
        block: v0.1.0  # If dependency is less than this, error.
        warn: v0.1.2  # If dependency is less than this, warn.
  - name: python
    packages:
      - name: Mopidy-Dirble
        block: v1.2.1
        warn: v1.2.2
  - name: go
    packages:
      - name: github.com/adrg/xdg
        block: v0.5.0
        warn: v0.6.0
  - name: nodejs
    packages:
      - name: react
        block: v17.0.3
        warn: v17.0.4

The --block/--no-block flag on rubrical grade overrides blocking_mode when given.

docs.title: Languages
docs.text:
Language declarations are minimums (e.g. requires-python = ">=3.10"), so rubrical grades the lowest version a declaration allows against warn and block. Every file that declares a version is graded and reported separately.

Language File Declaration python pyproject.toml project.requires-python, or tool.poetry.dependencies.python when requires-python isn't set. go go.mod The go directive. A go.mod without one is graded as go 1.16, which is what the Go toolchain assumes. nodejs package.json engines.node. python .python-version Every line, as uv reads it. A line may be a version (3.12) or a specifier set (>=3.12,<3.13). go .go-version The first word of every line, as goenv reads it. nodejs .node-version The first word of the file, as nodenv reads it. nodejs .nvmrc The single version left after removing # comments, as nvm reads it.

Each file is read with its ecosystem's own range syntax (PEP 440, Poetry, or npm). For example, >3.9 allows 3.9.1 in Python, while >18 means >=19.0.0 in npm.

  • Files that don't declare a version produce no result.
  • Declarations with no lower bound, such as "node": "*" or <3.12, and declarations that aren't valid in their syntax are reported as not gradeable rather than passing. Run with --debug to see why.
  • Pre-releases are graded by their release, so go 1.21rc1 is graded as 1.21.0.
  • A version file that lists several versions (pyenv and goenv make all of them available) is graded by the lowest one.
  • Version file entries that aren't versions, such as system, a virtualenv name, pypy3.10, cpython@3.12, lts/*, or latest, make that file not gradeable. Rubrical doesn't guess what an alias resolves to.

docs.title: Several reports on one PR
docs.text:
By default, rubrical keeps one comment per PR, so two rubrical runs on the same PR (for example, one per service in a monorepo, each with its own config) overwrite each other's comment. Give each run its own --report-id (or RUBRICAL_REPORT_ID) to keep a separate comment for each one:

rubrical grade --config services/api/rubrical.yaml --target services/api --report-id api ...
rubrical grade --config services/web/rubrical.yaml --target services/web --report-id web ...

A report ID is 1-100 characters of letters, digits, ., _, / or -. It's stored in a hidden marker in the comment and shown in the comment's heading. A run with a report ID only updates or deletes comments with the same ID. If it finds more than one (for example, after two runs raced each other), it keeps one and deletes the rest. A run without a report ID leaves comments with report IDs alone.

docs.title: 0001: Renovate weekly grouped updates with gated automerge
docs.text: Status: accepted (2026-10-24)

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Renovate ran every two weeks with a blanket automerge: true, but the repo had GitHub auto-merge turned off and no required checks, so green PRs sat waiting for the next Renovate run. CI flaked on bot PRs because arduino/setup-task called the GitHub API without authentication and hit the rate limit. And Renovate classes a Python runtime bump (3.14 → 3.15 in .python-version) as minor, so the blanket automerge could have moved the runtime without review if CI had happened to pass.

This follows tangle's setup (ADR 0013, ADR 0016). The full plan is in docs/agents/plans/renovate-weekly-grouped-updates.md.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Renovate runs on Fridays with a 5-day minimumReleaseAge.
  • One PR per ecosystem:
  • python: pep621, pyenv, the Dockerfile's dhi.io/python and ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv, and the devcontainer Python image. These move together on a runtime bump.
  • ci: GitHub Actions, plus regex-tracked pins in workflows.
  • devcontainer dependencies
  • Weekly lock file maintenance, in its own PR.
  • Everything automerges, majors included, except Python majors (pep621, pyenv, DHI, and the devcontainer Python image).
  • The Python runtime is capped at <3.15. Moving to 3.15 is a deliberate change: it bumps requires-python and the DHI and devcontainer tags, and it waits for 3.15 wheels (for example, cffi). Drop the cap as part of that change.
  • main has a ruleset that requires the main, docker, and pre-commit checks, and repo auto-merge is on. This lets Renovate's platformAutomerge merge as soon as CI passes.
  • Renovate authenticates to dhi.io with a DHI_TOKEN secret stored in the Mend developer portal.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• At most a handful of Renovate PRs a week, and most merge with no one touching them.
  • Python majors and the 3.15 runtime need a human.
  • If the DHI_TOKEN stops working, the dashboard shows a dhi.io lookup failure again. Rotate the Docker Hub token in the Mend portal.
  • Pins Renovate can't see on its own use the # <datasource>/<depName> comment convention in workflows.

docs.title: 0002: Scope GitHub report comments with an optional report ID
Context and Problem Statement
docs.text: report_github() finds its PR comment by the heading marker [Rubrical](https://github.com/ivanklee86/rubrical) Report, so every rubrical run on a PR shares one comment. Concurrent CI runs of our own live tests all write to PR #27 and clobber each other's comments, which caused the assert 2 == 1 and 404 Not Found flakes described in docs/agents/plans/harden-github-integration-tests.md. Users have the same problem in a monorepo that runs rubrical once per service on one PR: each run overwrites or deletes the others' comment. When duplicate comments do appear, the reporter edits the last one and never cleans up the rest.

docs.title: Considered Options
docs.text:
• A user-facing --report-id option (RUBRICAL_REPORT_ID) that scopes the comment with a hidden marker.
  • A test-only override of the marker string, applied by monkeypatching.
  • A fresh PR for each CI run instead of the shared PR #27.

docs.title: Decision Outcome
docs.text:
Chosen option: a user-facing --report-id. It fixes the test flakes through the real matching path, so the live tests still exercise production code, and it also serves the monorepo use case.

  • With a report ID, the comment starts with <!-- rubrical:report-id=<id> --> and its heading shows the ID. Only comments that start with exactly that marker match, so a comment that quotes the marker is never edited or deleted. The reporter converges duplicates: it keeps the oldest match and deletes the rest.
  • Without a report ID, matching is unchanged: heading marker present, and now also no report-ID marker, so legacy runs leave ID-scoped comments alone. Duplicate convergence is not applied to this legacy scope, so existing users with duplicate comments see no behavior change.
  • In both scopes, a 404 on edit falls back to creating a comment and a 404 on delete counts as done, instead of crashing the run.
  • A report ID is 1–100 characters from [A-Za-z0-9._/-], so it can't break out of the HTML comment.
  • Tests keep using the shared PR #27; each test gets a unique report ID and deletes only its own comments.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Good, because concurrent runs, whether in our CI or a user's monorepo, no longer interfere as long as their report IDs differ.
  • Good, because the reporter heals duplicates and concurrent deletes in the report-ID scope.
  • Neutral, because changing a run's report ID (or adding one) leaves the comment from the old scope behind; users have to delete it once.
  • Bad, because the legacy scope can still accumulate duplicates. Users who hit that can opt into a report ID.

docs.title: 0003: Check declared language versions as a separate construct
Context and Problem Statement
docs.text:
Rubrical grades dependency versions but not the language versions that a repository declares, such as requires-python = ">=3.7", go 1.19, or "engines": {"node": ">=18.0.0"}. Teams want to flag repositories that still allow end-of-life runtimes in the same way they flag outdated dependencies.

Two things make this different from dependency checks:

  • Languages and package managers don't map one-to-one. A Python version can be declared in pyproject.toml (PEP 621 or Poetry), uv.lock, .python-version, .tool-versions, runtime.txt, or a Dockerfile FROM line. Node.js has engines.node, .nvmrc, and .node-version. Several of these files aren't dependency manifests, and some (.tool-versions, Dockerfiles) declare several languages at once. A repository can also declare a language without using its package manager.
  • Language declarations are minimums. They are almost always lower bounds (>=3.7, ^3.12, go 1.19). The existing semver comparison grades the highest version a constraint allows: it returns NOOP for GT/GTE, turns ^3.12 into 3.999999.999999 (so it never warns), and treats a two-part version such as 1.19 as unparseable, which gives OK. As a result, none of the declarations in our fixtures can be graded today.

How should rubrical model language version checks?

docs.title: Considered Options
docs.text:
• A separate languages construct, with its own config section, its own discovery classes, and a lower-bound comparison.
  • Language checks inside each package manager, for example a language field on PackageManager config, read by the existing package manager classes.
  • The language as a synthetic package, for example packages: [{name: python, ...}] under the python package manager.

docs.title: Decision Outcome
docs.text:
Chosen option: a separate languages construct, because it is the only option that can read version sources outside dependency manifests, it keeps lower-bound semantics out of the dependency comparison path, and it doesn't collide with real package names (npm has a package called node).

  • Configuration. A new top-level languages list, with one warn/block pair per language. There is no type or packages list. Language versions are always graded as semver.
version: 1
languages:
  - name: python
    warn: v3.12.0
    block: v3.10.0
package_managers: []
  • Discovery. A rubrical/languages/ package with a BaseLanguage ABC and one subclass per language (python, go, nodejs). Each subclass lists the files it reads and extracts at most one version declaration from each file. File discovery (rglob plus the denylist) is extracted from BasePackageManager into a shared helper so both constructs use the same discovery code.
  • Comparison. A new lower-bound comparison grades the lowest version a declaration allows.
  • Within a set of AND-ed comparators, the highest lower bound applies. Across || alternatives, the lowest applies.
  • Versions are padded to three components, and pre-release suffixes are dropped.
  • The result is BLOCK if the lower bound is below block, otherwise WARN if it is below warn, otherwise OK. The existing results_to_status and max_status helpers are reused.
  • If no lower bound can be derived (for example * or <3.12) or the syntax is invalid, the result is NOOP, never OK, and the reason is logged with --debug.
  • Dialects. The parser takes a dialect (GO, PEP440, POETRY, or NPM), because the official specifications give the same text different meanings. For example, >3.9 allows 3.9.1 under PEP 440 and Poetry, but >1.2 means >=1.3.0 in npm. The rules for each dialect, with sources, are in the plan.
  • Absence. A file with no declaration for the language produces no result. It doesn't produce OK, so every package.json in a repository doesn't appear as a passing Node.js check. The exception is go.mod: the Go toolchain treats a missing go directive as go 1.16, so rubrical grades it as go 1.16 (implicit).
  • Unbounded declarations. npm documents "node": "*" as meaning the same as no declaration, so * and other declarations with no lower bound give NOOP rather than being graded as 0.0.0.
  • Several declarations. Each file is graded and reported on its own, the same way dependencies are graded per file. Rubrical doesn't try to reconcile conflicting declarations.
  • Results and reporting. Language results reuse PackageCheckResult, with name set to the language. They appear under a languages heading in the terminal and in the GitHub comment, and a language BLOCK counts toward the exit status like a dependency BLOCK.
  • Initial scope. go.mod (go directive), pyproject.toml (PEP 621 requires-python and Poetry tool.poetry.dependencies.python), and package.json (engines.node). Other version files are follow-ups. When a pyproject.toml declares both, requires-python is graded, because Poetry requires its python range to be a subset of requires-python.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Good, because language checks can grow to cover version files (.python-version, .nvmrc, .tool-versions, Dockerfiles) without changing the package manager model.
  • Good, because the lower-bound semantics are isolated, so the existing dependency comparisons don't change.
  • Good, because a language-only configuration works: package_managers becomes optional.
  • Neutral, because go.mod and pyproject.toml are read by both a package manager and a language class. Parsing stays in one place by sharing helpers, but the files are read twice per run.
  • Neutral, because configs jsonschema output changes. The new field is optional, so existing configurations remain valid.
  • Bad, because reporting one result per file can be noisy in monorepos with many package.json files. If this is a problem, a later change can add a per-language summary.

docs.text:

  • Test fixtures for engines.node are in tests/files/nodejs/engines/.

docs.title: Context and Problem Statement
docs.text:
ADR 0003 added language version checks for pyproject.toml, go.mod, and package.json, and listed version files as follow-ups. Many repositories pin their runtime only in a version manager's file: .python-version (pyenv, uv, setup-python), .node-version (nodenv, fnm, setup-node), .nvmrc (nvm, fnm, setup-node), or .go-version (goenv, setup-go). Those repositories currently get no language result at all.

Version files differ from the manifests that ADR 0003 covers:

  • They pin a version rather than declare a range. 3.12 in .python-version means "use the newest 3.12.x", not "3.12 or newer". The lowest version the pin allows is still the right thing to grade, because it is the runtime the repository will use.
  • Each tool has its own format. None of them is a range syntax that ADR 0003 already parses. pyenv and goenv read one version per line and use all of them. uv reads a whole line, also accepts PEP 440 specifiers (>=3.12,<3.13), and ignores lines that start with #. nvm strips # comments anywhere in a line, allows exactly one version, and accepts aliases (lts/*, node). nodenv reads only the first word of .node-version.
  • Their contents are often not versions. system, virtualenv names, pypy3.10, cpython@3.12, lts/iron, and latest are all valid in at least one tool.

How should rubrical read these files?

docs.title: Considered Options
docs.text:
• New sources in the existing language classes, with a new dialect for bare version files.
  • Reuse the existing dialects (npm for Node.js files, PEP 440 for .python-version, Go for .go-version).
  • A new construct for version-manager files, separate from languages.

docs.title: Decision Outcome
docs.text:
Chosen option: new sources in the existing language classes, with a new dialect, because the files declare the same thing that the language checks already grade, so they share the languages config, thresholds, and reporting. Reusing existing dialects would accept syntax the tools reject (>=18 || ^16 in .nvmrc) or reject syntax they accept (a bare 3.12 isn't valid PEP 440).

  • Files. python also reads .python-version, nodejs also reads .node-version and .nvmrc, and go also reads .go-version. Each file is graded and reported on its own, the same as in ADR 0003, so a repository with both pyproject.toml and .python-version gets two Python rows.
  • Out of scope. .tool-versions (asdf and mise), mise.toml, .python-versions, runtime.txt, uv.lock, and Dockerfiles. .tool-versions declares several languages in one file and can be added later without changing this design.
  • Reading each file. Each file is read the way the tool that owns it reads it:
  • .python-version: every line, trimmed, skipping blank lines and lines that start with # (uv).
  • .go-version: the first word of every line, skipping blank lines and lines that start with # (goenv).
  • .node-version: the first word of the file (nodenv).
  • .nvmrc: # and everything after it is removed, lines are trimmed, blank lines and key=value lines are skipped, and exactly one line must remain (nvm).
  • New dialects.
  • VERSION_FILE, used by .node-version, .nvmrc, and .go-version. Each line is a bare version: an optional v, then release numbers, then an optional pre-release suffix. Operators, wildcards, and anything else are not gradeable.
  • PYTHON_VERSION_FILE, used by .python-version. Each line is a bare version, as above, or a PEP 440 specifier set, which uv accepts. Implementation-prefixed requests (pypy3.10, cpython@3.12, cpython-3.12.3-macos-aarch64-none) are not gradeable.
  • Several versions in one file. pyenv and goenv make every listed version available, so the lowest version is graded, which is the same rule as || alternatives in ADR 0003.
  • Not gradeable means NOOP. If any line can't be graded (system, a virtualenv name, pypy3.10, lts/*, latest), the whole file is NOOP, and the reason is logged with --debug. One ungradeable line makes the lowest version unknown, so grading the other lines would risk a silent OK. This matches the ADR 0003 rule that an unbounded || alternative makes the whole declaration ungradeable.
  • Empty files. A file with no version lines (empty, or only comments) produces no result, the same as a manifest that doesn't declare a version.
  • Reporting. raw_constraint is the file name and each version, quoted, such as .python-version "3.12" "3.11".

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Good, because repositories that pin a runtime only in a version file are now graded.
  • Good, because each file follows its own tool's rules, so rubrical doesn't grade content the tool would read differently.
  • Neutral, because pins and minimums share thresholds. A pin of 3.12 and a minimum of >=3.12 both grade as 3.12.0, which is the intended meaning of a threshold.
  • Bad, because a repository that pins lts/* or system is reported as NOOP, and a reviewer has to use --debug to see why. This is preferred over guessing which version an alias currently resolves to.
  • Bad, because more rows per repository adds to the monorepo noise noted in ADR 0003.

docs.title: Rubrical internals
docs.text: Rubrical is a Typer CLI that scans a repository for dependency manifests, compares each declared dependency version constraint and each declared language version against warn/block thresholds from a config file, and reports results to the terminal and, optionally, to a GitHub PR comment.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text: Path Role rubrical/main.py Typer app. grade command plus the mounted configs sub-app. Entry point is rubrical = rubrical.main:app. rubrical/subcommands/configs.py configs validate and configs jsonschema. rubrical/rubrical.py Rubrical orchestrator, PACKAGE_MANAGER_MAPPING and LANGUAGE_MAPPING (config name → class). rubrical/package_managers/ BasePackageManager ABC plus one subclass per ecosystem (go, jsonnet, nodejs, python). rubrical/languages/ BaseLanguage ABC plus one subclass per language (go, nodejs, python). Each extracts at most one LanguageDeclaration per file. version_files.py reads version manager files (.python-version, .go-version, .node-version, .nvmrc) the way each owning tool does. docs.text:

docs.title: Core data model
docs.text:
• Config (Pydantic, schemas/configuration.py): RubricalConfig{version, blocking_mode, languages[] = [], package_managers[] = []}. PackageManager{name: SupportedPackageManagers, packages[]} → PackageRequirement{name, type=semver|generic, warn, block}. LanguageRequirement{name: SupportedLanguages, warn, block}; each language may appear once. The config is loaded from .yaml, .json, or .toml with benedict.
  • Parsed dependency (dataclass, schemas/package.py): Package{name, raw_constraint, version_constraints: [Specification{version, specifier: DependencySpecifications}]}. A single dependency can carry several specifications, such as >=1.0,<2.
  • Language declaration (dataclass, schemas/language.py): LanguageDeclaration{version, raw_constraint, dialect: VersionDialect}. version is the declared range (>=3.7); raw_constraint is what reports show (requires-python ">=3.7").
  • Result (dataclass, schemas/results.py): PackageCheckResult{name, file, check: PackageCheck, version_package, version_warn, version_block}.
  • PackageCheck has four values: OK, WARN, BLOCK, and NOOP. NOOP means the constraint can't be judged, for example a lower bound only.

docs.title: Package manager pattern
docs.text:
Each subclass of BasePackageManager:

  1. Sets the class attributes target_files (glob names) and, optionally, denylist_pathnames, which are substring-matched against the path.
  2. Sets self.name = SupportedPackageManagers.X.value in __init__.
  3. Optionally extends self.specification_symbols with a dict merge (|) to map ecosystem operators. Python adds ~=→APPROX_EQ. NodeJS adds ~→APPROX_EQ and ^→COMPATIBLE.
  4. Implements parse_package_manager_file(details), which must initialize and fill self.packages[details.name]. details.name is the file path relative to --target.
  5. Optionally overrides normalize_name(name). It is applied to both the config name and the parsed name before matching. The default keeps names exact; Python applies PEP 503 rules (lowercase, with runs of -, _ and . treated as -).

match_from_specification_symbols(version) finds the specifier by substring match. The last matching group wins, so >= resolves to GTE rather than GT. The function then strips the operator characters. If nothing matches, the specifier defaults to EQ.

Manager Files Parsing notes go go.mod Regex over ( … ) blocks. Lines containing indirect are skipped. Every entry is EQ. jsonnet jsonnetfile.json Pydantic models for the file. The name comes from git.repository_from_url(remote) as owner/repo. The version (which may be a branch) is EQ. python requirements.txt, pyproject.toml requirements-parser for each line. In pyproject.toml, PEP 621 project.dependencies are re-parsed through requirements.parse. Poetry (tool.poetry) goes through requirements_detector.find_requirements(parent_dir). Requirements with no version specifier are dropped. nodejs package.json (skips node_modules) Reads dependencies, devDependencies, and peerDependencies. Whitespace between an operator and its version is removed first (>= 1.2.3 → >=1.2.3), and runs of whitespace between comparators are collapsed. Partial versions and X-ranges (1, 1.2, 1.x, 1.x.x, 1.2.*) become APPROX_EQ. a - b becomes GTE+LTE. Two-part >=a <b is parsed per part. \|\| and other multi-part ranges are skipped.

docs.title: Language pattern
docs.text:
Each subclass of BaseLanguage sets target_files, optionally denylist_pathnames, sets self.name = SupportedLanguages.X.value, and implements parse_file(details) -> Optional[LanguageDeclaration]. Returning None means the file declares no version, and it produces no result.

Language Files Declaration Dialect go go.mod The go directive. Without one, go 1.16 (implicit), as the Go toolchain assumes. toolchain is ignored. GO go .go-version The first word of every non-comment line (goenv). VERSION_FILE python pyproject.toml (skips .venv, node_modules) project.requires-python, else tool.poetry.dependencies.python. PEP440 / POETRY python .python-version (skips .venv, node_modules) Every trimmed non-comment line (uv). PYTHON_VERSION_FILE nodejs package.json (skips node_modules) engines.node. NPM nodejs .node-version (skips node_modules) The first word of the file (nodenv). VERSION_FILE nodejs .nvmrc (skips node_modules) Lines left after removing # comments and key=value lines, joined by spaces, so more than one version isn't gradeable (nvm). VERSION_FILE

Version files dispatch on file_details.path.name in parse_file. version holds one entry per line (joined by newlines) and raw_constraint quotes each entry after the file name, for example .python-version "3.12" "3.9". A version file with no entries returns None.

docs.title: Comparison semantics (comparisons/)
docs.text:
• semver (default): each Specification reduces to the highest version the constraint allows, which is then compared against the thresholds:
  • EQ, LT, and LTE use the version as-is.
  • GT, GTE, and NE give NOOP.
  • APPROX_EQ pads missing components with 999999, so 1.2 becomes 1.2.999999.
  • COMPATIBLE replaces the last component with 999999 and pads, so 6.0.1 becomes 6.0.999999.

A leading v is stripped. The result is BLOCK if the version is below block, otherwise WARN if it is below warn, otherwise OK. A ValueError from semver (an unparseable version) gives OK. For a package with several specifications, max_status picks the most severe in the order BLOCK > WARN > OK > NOOP. - generic: applies only when there is exactly one EQ specification; anything else gives NOOP. It uses a plain lexicographic string comparison (warn > version, block > version). - Language lower bound (lower_bound.py): languages are graded by the lowest MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH their declaration allows, because language declarations are minimums. The rules per dialect, with sources, are in the plan. - Whitespace after an operator is removed. Within AND-ed comparators the highest lower bound applies; across || alternatives the lowest applies. - Versions are padded to three parts and pre-release/post/dev/build suffixes are dropped (1.21rc1 → 1.21.0). - >X differs by dialect: PEP 440 and Poetry give the next patch (>3.9 → 3.9.1); npm increments the last given part (>1.2 → 1.3.0, >1.2.3 → 1.2.4). - Version file dialects treat each line as an alternative, so the lowest line applies. VERSION_FILE lines must be bare versions (optional v, no operator or wildcard). PYTHON_VERSION_FILE lines may also be PEP 440 specifier sets. One ungradeable line (system, lts/*, pypy3.10) makes the whole file NOOP. - lower_bound() raises UngradeableError when there is no lower bound (*, <3.12) or the syntax is invalid in the dialect (^ in PEP 440). compare_language() turns that into NOOP, never OK, and returns a LanguageGrade whose reason is logged with --debug.

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text:
• Terminal: one table per manager, plus a languages table when languages are configured, listing only WARN and BLOCK results and printed only when there is at least one. Otherwise a single success line is printed.
  • Result keys: check_all() returns results keyed by languages (only when configured, first) and then by package manager name. Both reporters loop over the keys. Language blocks and warnings count toward the exit status like dependency ones.
  • Exit status: should_block is the --block/--no-block flag when given, otherwise blocking_mode from the config (default true). Blocks with should_block exit 1. Blocks without it print a "blocking is disabled" header and exit 0.
  • GitHub: enabled when RUBRICAL_GH_TOKEN is set. It also needs RUBRICAL_REPOSITORY and RUBRICAL_PR_ID, and optionally RUBRICAL_GH_CUSTOM_URL (which uses <url>/api/v3) and RUBRICAL_REPORT_ID (--report-id). | in a declaration is escaped as \| so || ranges stay in their table cell. If there are warnings or blocks, the comment is edited or created. If the run is clean, any old comment is deleted. Comments are matched within a scope (ADR 0002):
  • With a report ID: comments that start with <!-- rubrical:report-id=<id> --> (a comment that only quotes the marker further down is ignored). Duplicates converge: the oldest match is kept and the rest are deleted.
  • Without a report ID (legacy): comments containing [Rubrical](https://github.com/ivanklee86/rubrical) Report and no report-ID marker. The last match is used and any others are left alone, as before.
  • In both scopes, a 404 on edit() (the comment was deleted concurrently) falls back to creating a new comment, and a 404 on delete() counts as done. Every comment ID found, created, edited or deleted is logged through the rubrical.reporters.gh logger.

docs.title: Common changes
docs.text:
Add a package manager 1. Add a value to SupportedPackageManagers in enum.py. 2. Create package_managers/<name>.py that subclasses BasePackageManager. 3. Register the class in PACKAGE_MANAGER_MAPPING in rubrical.py. 4. Add fixtures under tests/files/<name>/ and a test in tests/unit/package_managers/. Add entries to tests/files/rubrical*.yaml if integration coverage is wanted.

Add a language 1. Add a value to SupportedLanguages in enum.py, and to VersionDialect if its version syntax is new (then add a comparator and an alternatives splitter to DIALECTS in comparisons/lower_bound.py, following the official spec). 2. Create languages/<name>.py that subclasses BaseLanguage. 3. Register the class in LANGUAGE_MAPPING in rubrical.py. 4. Add fixtures under tests/files/, parser cases to tests/unit/comparisons/test_lower_bound.py, a test in tests/unit/languages/, and expected results to tests/files/rubrical-languages.yaml and test_rubrical_languages.

Add a version file for an existing language 1. Add a reader to languages/version_files.py that follows the owning tool's source, and returns one entry per version. 2. Add the file name to the language's target_files and dispatch on it in parse_file, using version_files.declaration() with VERSION_FILE (or a new dialect if lines can hold ranges). 3. Add fixtures under tests/files/version-files/, reader cases to tests/unit/languages/test_language_version_files.py, and expected results to test_rubrical_languages.

Add a comparison type 1. Add a value to PackageTypes. 2. Create a module in comparisons/ that returns PackageCheck. Use utils.results_to_status and utils.max_status. 3. Add a branch for it in comparisons/__init__.check_package.

docs.title: Dev workflow
docs.text:
• Tooling is uv and Task. The commands are:
  • task python:install
  • task python:fmt, which runs ruff format and ruff check --fix
  • task python:lint, which runs ruff and ty check
  • task python:test, which runs pytest tests/unit tests/integration
  • task docs:test, which runs mkdocs build --strict
  • Tests use fixture repos in tests/files/. Unit tests instantiate a manager, then call read_package_manager_files(path) and parse_package_manager_files(), then assert on .packages[relpath]. Integration tests drive main.app through typer.testing.CliRunner with --target tests/. The GitHub reporter's logic is unit tested offline in tests/unit/reporters/test_gh.py against an in-memory fake of PyGithub. Live GitHub tests are marked github, need RUBRICAL_TEST_GITHUB_ACCESS_TOKEN (without it they skip, and -rs lists them), and target PR #27 of ivanklee86/rubrical. They use the github_report fixture in tests/fixtures.py, which gives each test a unique report ID (test-<run id>-<attempt>-<test>-<random>), so concurrent CI runs never touch each other's comments. The fixture deletes only that test's comments at teardown, and at setup it sweeps test- comments older than 6 hours that were left by cancelled runs. Run pytest -o log_cli=true -m github to watch the comment IDs each test touches.
  • The version comes from setuptools_scm and is written to rubrical/_version.py, which is untracked. The Docker image (Dockerfile) uses ENTRYPOINT ["rubrical", "grade"].

docs.title: Known quirks
docs.text:
• Unparseable semver versions (such as branch names) are treated as OK, not NOOP. Language checks don't share this quirk.
  • go.mod, pyproject.toml and package.json are read twice when both a package manager and a language are configured.
  • Package names are matched exactly for every manager except Python, so a capitalization difference in a Node.js, Go or Jsonnet name won't match.

docs.title: Harden the GitHub integration tests against shared-state failures
docs.text: Status: implemented (2026-10-24), except step 6, which is manual. Decisions are recorded in ADR 0002.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: The tests that talk to GitHub (tests/unit/reporters/test_gh.py::test_gh_report, ::test_gh_cleanup, ::test_gh_report_noop, and tests/integration/test_cli.py::test_cli_gh_report) all read and write comments on one shared, long-lived PR, ivanklee86/rubrical#27. Every CI run that has RUBRICAL_TEST_GITHUB_ACCESS_TOKEN runs them against that PR. Renovate routinely opens or rebases several PRs within seconds of each other, so several CI runs mutate PR #27 at the same time.

docs.title: Evidence from prior runs
docs.text:
Run Started (UTC) Failure 40081234910 2026-10-24 09:15:27 test_cli_gh_report: assert 2 == 1 (two Rubrical comments). Overlapped runs 40081245491 (09:15:36) and 40081274745 (09:16:03). 40079708135 2026-10-24 08:52:08 test_gh_report: 404 Not Found on update an issue comment; test_cli_gh_report: assert 2 == 1. Overlapped three other runs started 08:51:33–08:52:04. 40077848308 2026-10-24 08:23:28 test_gh_report: assert 2 == 1. Overlapped four other runs started 08:23:07–08:23:38. 40077826932 2026-10-24 08:23:07 test_cli_gh_report setup error: 404 Not Found on delete an issue comment.

(The remaining failures in that window were lint, ty, and Docker build failures, which are unrelated.)

At the time of writing, PR #27 still has a leftover Rubrical comment (id 6382555631, created 09:28:36) from the last green run on main, which shows that the tests don't clean up even when they pass.

docs.title: Root causes
docs.text:
1. Shared mutable fixture across concurrent runs. All runs use the same PR and the same fixed comment marker ([Rubrical](https://github.com/ivanklee86/rubrical) Report), so run A's comment is indistinguishable from run B's. That leads to three race outcomes:
  2. Both runs see no comment and both create one, so the count is 2.
  3. Run B's github_pr_clean fixture deletes run A's comment between A's lookup and A's edit() or delete(), so A gets a 404.
  4. Run B's fixture tries to delete a comment that run A's fixture already deleted, so B gets a 404 during setup.
  5. Setup-only cleanup, no teardown. github_pr_clean (tests/fixtures.py) deletes every comment on the PR before the test and nothing after it. test_gh_report_noop and test_cli_gh_report leave a live comment behind on every run, which the next run has to clean up and might race on.
  6. Cleanup isn't idempotent. issue_comment.delete() raises UnknownObjectException when the comment is already gone. Because this runs during fixture setup, the test errors before it starts.
  7. Over-broad cleanup. The fixture deletes all comments on the PR, including other runs' in-flight comments and any human comments, rather than only what the current test created.
  8. Sleep-based pacing. time.sleep(5) after each delete slows the suite and widens the race window. It doesn't wait for anything specific.
  9. Assertions match too broadly. "Rubrical" in issue_comment.body counts any comment that mentions the word, not just reports from this run.

docs.title: Product behavior worth flagging
docs.text: report_github() in rubrical/reporters/gh.py keeps the last comment that matches the marker and ignores any others. When duplicates exist, whether from these races or from a real user who runs rubrical twice in parallel, rubrical never converges back to one comment, and cleanup only deletes one of them. I don't want tests that enshrine this behavior. Step 3 proposes changing it.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• A GitHub test failure means rubrical's GitHub reporting is broken, not that another CI run happened to overlap.
  • Each test removes everything it created, even when it fails partway through.
  • Most of the reporter's logic is covered without network access, so it runs on forks and locally without a token.
  • GitHub calls made by tests can be traced: each comment can be linked back to the run that created it, and created and deleted comment IDs are logged.

docs.title: 1. Isolate each run's comments with a report ID (product change)
docs.text:
Add an optional report identifier to the GitHub reporter: a --report-id option on grade, with the environment variable RUBRICAL_REPORT_ID. When it is set, the comment body includes a hidden marker <!-- rubrical:report-id=<id> -->, and report_github() matches only comments that carry that marker. When it is unset, behavior is unchanged: the comment is matched by the existing heading marker, so existing users keep their current comments.

This also has standalone user value. A monorepo that runs rubrical several times on one PR (for example, once per service with different configs) currently has its runs overwrite each other's comment. With report IDs, each run gets its own comment.

Record the decision as an ADR in docs/adrs/0002-github-report-id.md and update the Reporting section of docs/agents/internals.md and the user docs.

docs.title: 2. Rewrite the live-GitHub fixture around ownership and teardown
docs.text:
Replace github_pr_clean in tests/fixtures.py with a github_report fixture that:

  • Generates a unique report ID per test invocation: f"test-{GITHUB_RUN_ID or 'local'}-{GITHUB_RUN_ATTEMPT or 0}-{request.node.name}-{uuid4().hex[:8]}".
  • Yields (pr, report_id).
  • In teardown, which runs even when the test fails, deletes only comments whose body contains that report ID. It treats UnknownObjectException (404) as success.
  • At setup, sweeps comments with a rubrical:report-id=test- marker that are older than a set age (for example, 6 hours). This cleans up after runs that were cancelled or hit a timeout before their teardown ran. The sweep never touches comments without a test marker, and it never touches young comments that may belong to a run still in progress.
  • Logs each comment ID it creates, finds or deletes, together with the report ID, through the logging module, so pytest -o log_cli=true and the CI log show exactly what each run did to PR #27.

Embed the CI run URL ($GITHUB_SERVER_URL/$GITHUB_REPOSITORY/actions/runs/$GITHUB_RUN_ID) in test-created comments so that someone looking at PR #27 can tell which run left a stray comment. This can go in the report ID itself or in a second hidden marker that only tests set.

Remove time.sleep(5). Where a test needs to observe a write, use a small wait_for(predicate, timeout=30, interval=1) helper that polls pr.get_issue_comments() until the expected count is reached. This copes with GitHub's eventual consistency without fixed sleeps.

~~Configure PyGithub with a custom urllib3.Retry in tests.~~ Dropped during implementation: PyGithub 2.x already defaults to GithubRetry(total=10), which retries 5xx responses and rate limits.

docs.title: 3. Make the reporter converge on a single comment
docs.text:
Within one match scope (one report ID, or the legacy marker when there is no ID), change report_github() so it:

  • Collects all matching comments, not just the last one.
  • When reporting, edits the first match and deletes the rest.
  • When the run is clean, deletes all matches.
  • Treats a 404 on edit() (another process deleted the comment) by creating a new comment, and a 404 on delete() as already done.

This makes the reporter self-heal from duplicates, whatever caused them.

docs.title: 4. Move most GitHub coverage off the network
docs.text:
Split tests/unit/reporters/test_gh.py into the following:

  • Unit tests (no network). Fake Github / Repository / PullRequest / IssueComment objects (for example, unittest.mock with a small in-memory comment list, or the responses library pinned to an exact version), injected by monkeypatching rubrical.reporters.gh.Github. Planned cases:
  • Happy path: no existing comment and findings present, so one comment is created.
  • Upsert: an existing comment and findings present, so that comment is edited and no new one is created.
  • Cleanup: an existing comment and a clean run, so the comment is deleted.
  • No-op: no comment and a clean run, so there are no write calls and the message says "Nothing to report".
  • Duplicates: two matching comments, so one is edited and the other deleted (step 3).
  • Race on edit: edit() raises 404, so a new comment is created.
  • Race on delete: delete() raises 404, so no error is raised.
  • Scoping: with report ID a set, a comment with report ID b and a legacy comment without an ID are both left alone.
  • Legacy compatibility: with no report ID, the existing heading-marker comment is still found and edited.
  • Custom URL: with custom_url set, Github is constructed with base_url=<url>/api/v3.
  • Live integration tests (network, token required). Keep one live round trip in tests/integration/test_github.py: create, then upsert, then clean, with the CLI test_cli_gh_report as a second test. Both use the github_report fixture and are marked @pytest.mark.github (register the marker in pyproject.toml). Delete test_gh_report_noop. It asserts nothing and leaks a comment.

Tighten assertions to count comments whose body contains this test's report ID, rather than "Rubrical" in body.

docs.title: 5. CI changes
docs.text:
• Add workflow-level concurrency: { group: ci-${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}, cancel-in-progress: true } to .github/workflows/ci.yaml. Renovate force-pushes made renovate/lock-file-maintenance-python run CI four times in 12 minutes, and superseded runs should be cancelled. This reduces load. It is not what makes the tests correct; step 1 does that.
  • Keep the GitHub tests in the same pytest invocation so coverage still includes them, but add -rs so skipped GitHub tests show up in the log, for example on fork PRs that have no secret.
  • I'm not proposing a single global concurrency group to serialize the GitHub tests across runs. GitHub keeps at most one pending job per concurrency group and cancels older pending ones, so a burst of Renovate PRs would get cancelled jobs, which are effectively failures. With per-run report IDs it isn't needed.

docs.title: 6. One-off cleanup
docs.text: After steps 1–4 merge, delete the leftover comment(s) on PR #27 by hand (gh api -X DELETE repos/ivanklee86/rubrical/issues/comments/<id>). After that, the age-based sweep in step 2 keeps the PR tidy.

docs.title: Order of work
docs.text:
1. Steps 3 and 4 (unit half): reporter convergence and the offline unit tests. These have no product-surface change and can ship on their own. Together with a fixture teardown that ignores 404s, they already remove the 404 failures.
  2. Step 1, with its ADR and docs: the report-ID option.
  3. Step 2 and the live half of step 4: the new fixture and the rewritten live tests. Together with step 1, these remove the 2 == 1 failures.
  4. Step 5: CI concurrency and -rs.
  5. Step 6: manual cleanup.

docs.title: Decisions (formerly open questions)
docs.text:
Answered on 2026-10-24:

  • User-facing --report-id: yes. Implemented as --report-id / RUBRICAL_REPORT_ID.
  • Duplicate convergence in the legacy (no report ID) path: no. It applies only when a report ID is set. The legacy path keeps using the last match and leaves the others alone. The 404 tolerance on edit and delete applies to both paths, since it only replaces a crash.
  • Fresh PR per run: no. Tests keep using PR #27, isolated by report ID.

The original questions:

  • Is a user-facing --report-id acceptable? The alternative that avoids a product change is a test-only override of the marker string through monkeypatching. It works, but then the live tests no longer exercise the real matching path, and the monorepo use case goes unaddressed.
  • Should the duplicate convergence in step 3 also apply to the legacy (no report ID) path? I think yes, but it changes current behavior for users who already have duplicate comments: rubrical would start deleting the extras.
  • Should we create a fresh PR per CI run instead of reusing PR #27? It gives the strongest isolation, but it needs contents: write to push a branch, and it adds API calls and leaves branches to clean up. I don't recommend it unless report IDs prove insufficient.

docs.title: Check declared language versions
docs.text: Status: implemented (2026-10-24). See Implementation notes for where the code differs from this plan. Decisions are recorded in ADR 0003.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Rubrical grades dependency versions but not the language versions that a repository declares. Teams want to warn or block when a repository still allows an end-of-life runtime, such as requires-python = ">=3.7" or go 1.19.

The existing semver comparison can't grade these declarations, because it grades the highest version that a constraint allows, and language declarations are minimums. Here is what each fixture gets today:

Fixture Declaration Today's result Why tests/files/python/pyproject.toml requires-python = ">=3.7" NOOP GTE always gives NOOP. tests/files/uv/pyproject.toml requires-python = ">=3.14" NOOP Same. tests/files/poetry/pyproject.toml python = "^3.12" always OK COMPATIBLE becomes 3.999999.999999. tests/files/go/go.mod go 1.19 always OK semver.compare("1.19", …) raises ValueError, which is treated as OK. tests/files/nodejs/engines/*/package.json engines.node not read The Node.js package manager only reads dependency sections.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• Users can set a warn and block threshold for each language and get results for every file that declares that language's version.
  • A language check is never silently OK. If a declaration can't be graded, the result is NOOP, and the reason is logged with --debug.
  • Dependency checks don't change at all.
  • Every result can be traced back to the file and the raw declaration it came from.

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
• Version files that aren't dependency manifests: .python-version, .nvmrc, .node-version, .tool-versions, runtime.txt, Dockerfiles, go.work. The design supports them, and they are follow-ups.
  • The Go toolchain directive. Only the go directive is graded.
  • Reconciling conflicting declarations across files.
  • Fixing the existing dependency comparison bugs listed under Related findings.

docs.title: 1. Configuration
docs.text:

docs.title: 2. Shared file discovery
docs.text: Extract the rglob and denylist loop in BasePackageManager.read_package_manager_files() into a function in rubrical/utilities/files.py. It should return Dict[str, FileDetails], keyed by the path relative to the target. Rename PackageManagerFileDetails to FileDetails and keep the old name as an alias, so the package manager code changes as little as possible. BasePackageManager then calls the helper. Its behavior doesn't change, and the existing package manager tests cover it.

docs.title: 3. Language classes
docs.text:
Create rubrical/languages/:

  • base_language.py: BaseLanguage ABC with name, target_files, denylist_pathnames, found_files, and declarations: Dict[str, Package]. It provides read_files(target), which uses the shared helper, and parse_files(), which calls the abstract parse_file(details) -> Optional[Package] and stores only the files that return a declaration. Each declaration is a Package with name set to the language and raw_constraint set to the declared value, as written in the file.
  • go.py: reads go.mod, with dialect GO. It matches the ^go\s+(\S+) line. If there's no go directive, it records go 1.16 (implicit). It ignores toolchain.
  • python.py: reads pyproject.toml. It reads project.requires-python with dialect PEP440, or failing that tool.poetry.dependencies.python with dialect POETRY. Denylist: .venv, node_modules.
  • nodejs.py: reads package.json, specifically engines.node, with dialect NPM. Denylist: node_modules.

Each declaration carries its dialect, either as a field on a small LanguageDeclaration dataclass that wraps Package, or as a new optional field on Package. I'll decide which when implementing; the wrapper is preferred so dependency code doesn't see the new field.

Add LANGUAGE_MAPPING next to PACKAGE_MANAGER_MAPPING in rubrical/rubrical.py.

docs.title: 4. Lower-bound comparison
docs.text:
Add rubrical/comparisons/lower_bound.py with two functions:

  • lower_bound(raw: str, dialect: Dialect) -> Optional[str] takes the raw declaration and returns a three-component version, or None. Dialect is GO, PEP440, POETRY, or NPM. A dialect is needed because the same text means different things in different ecosystems (see Verified syntax rules). Each language class picks the dialect for each source it reads.
  • compare_language(requirement, declaration) -> PackageCheck returns NOOP when lower_bound returns None. Otherwise it compares the bound with results_to_status().

The algorithm is the same for every dialect. Only the tokenizing and the meaning of each operator differ.

  1. Remove whitespace between an operator and its version. All three range syntaxes allow it, for example >= 3.8 and > 1.2.3 < 1.2.5. Then split the range into alternatives and split each alternative into comparators. Alternatives are separated by || in npm, and by || or | in Poetry. PEP 440 has no OR. Comparators are separated by whitespace in npm, commas in PEP 440, and either in Poetry.
  2. For each comparator, derive its lower bound using the rules in the table. If a comparator has only an upper bound (<, <=, !=), it contributes nothing.
  3. An alternative's lower bound is the highest lower bound among its comparators, because comparators are combined with AND. An alternative with no lower bound is unbounded.
  4. The declaration's lower bound is the lowest lower bound across its alternatives. If any alternative is unbounded, the whole declaration is unbounded, so the function returns None.
  5. Pad to MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH and drop any pre-release, dev, or post suffix, keeping only the release numbers: 1.21rc1 becomes 1.21.0, 3.13.0rc1 becomes 3.13.0, and 20.0.0-rc.1 becomes 20.0.0.
  6. If a token is invalid in the dialect, the function returns None and logs the reason with --debug. Examples: ^ or || in PEP 440, ~=3 in PEP 440, a wildcard with an ordered operator in PEP 440 (>=3.*), === arbitrary equality, or text that isn't a version at all.

I'm writing a small parser rather than adding packaging or an npm-range library. No one library handles Go, PEP 440, Poetry, and npm syntax, and only the lower bound is needed. If the parser grows past the rules below, we should revisit that choice.

docs.title: Verified syntax rules
docs.text:
These rules were checked against the official documentation on 2026-10-24. Sources are listed at the end of the plan.

Rule Go PEP 440 (requires-python) Poetry (python) npm (engines.node) Meaning of the declaration Minimum toolchain version. Enforced since Go 1.21. Supported Python versions. Supported Python versions for locking. It must be a subset of requires-python. Supported Node.js versions. Advisory unless engine-strict is set. Operators None. It's a bare version. ~= == != <= >= < > === PEP 440 operators plus ^ and ~ < <= > >= = plus ^, ~, hyphen ranges, and X-ranges AND / OR Not applicable Comma / none Comma or whitespace / \|\| or \| Whitespace / \|\| >X lower bound Not applicable Next patch: >3.9 gives 3.9.1, because PEP 440 says >1.7 allows 1.7.1 Next patch: >3.9 gives 3.9.1. Poetry builds an exclusive range on the padded version. Increment the last given component: >1 gives 2.0.0, >1.2 gives 1.3.0, and >1.2.3 gives 1.2.4. node-semver's replaceXRange and minVersion do this. Bare partial version 1.19 is the language version, ordered just before 1.19.0, so it gives 1.19.0 ==3.12 pads to 3.12.0 3.12 is exact and pads to 3.12.0 20 is an X-range (>=20.0.0 <21.0.0-0), so it gives 20.0.0 Wildcards Not applicable Only with == and !=: ==3.12.* gives 3.12.0 * means any version, and 3.* gives 3.0.0 *, x, "" mean any version, and 20.x gives 20.0.0 Leading v / = Not applicable v is ignored Same as PEP 440 Both are stripped Missing declaration Treated as go 1.16 No result No result No result. npm documents a missing value the same as *.

docs.title: What counts as acceptable
docs.text:
These decisions follow from the rules above.

  • Gradeable: any declaration whose lower bound can be derived with these rules.
  • NOOP, logged with --debug: a declaration with no lower bound, such as *, "", <3.12, !=3.9.*, or ^18 || <16. npm documents * as meaning the same as no declaration, so grading it as 0.0.0 and blocking would contradict the docs. This is a deliberate difference from node-semver's minVersion, which returns 0.0.0 for these ranges.
  • NOOP, logged with --debug: syntax that is invalid in the dialect. The tool that owns the file would reject it anyway.
  • Pre-releases: graded by their release numbers, so 1.21rc1 is graded as 1.21.0. A release candidate only precedes its own release, so this doesn't hide an end-of-life version.
  • Go with no go directive: graded as 1.16, with raw_constraint set to go 1.16 (implicit). This is what the Go toolchain does, and it's the one case where a missing declaration produces a result.
  • Go toolchain directive: ignored. The docs say it is only a suggestion and can't be lower than the go version.
  • Python with both PEP 621 and Poetry: grade requires-python. Poetry requires its python range to be a subset of requires-python, so requires-python is the minimum that users actually see.

docs.title: 5. Orchestration and reporting
docs.text:
In Rubrical:

  • Add check_languages() -> List[PackageCheckResult]. For each configured language, it reads and parses files, then appends a PackageCheckResult(name=language, file=file, check=…, version_package=raw_constraint, version_warn=…, version_block=…) for each declaration.
  • check_package_managers() becomes check_all(), or gains a languages pass, that also runs check_languages(). It calls terminal.terminal_report("languages", results), stores the results under the languages key in the results dict, and folds them into warnings_found and blocks_found.
  • Only add the languages key when languages are configured, so GitHub comments from existing configs don't change.

reporters/gh.py and reporters/terminal.py need no changes. They already loop over the result keys, and the "update to >= warn" wording also works for languages. The table column is labeled "Dependency". I'll check whether it reads oddly for languages, and if so rename it to "Name".

docs.title: 6. Observability
docs.text:
With --debug, log:

  • Each file that a language class reads, and whether it found a declaration.
  • Each raw declaration, the lower bound derived from it, and the result.
  • The reason for each NOOP (no lower bound, or unparseable version), so it's always clear why a file wasn't graded.

docs.title: Test cases
docs.text:
tests/unit/comparisons/test_lower_bound.py, for lower_bound(). Each case comes from an example in the official docs, or applies a documented rule:

  • Go:
  • 1.19 gives 1.19.0, 1.21.3 gives 1.21.3, and 1.21rc1 gives 1.21.0.
  • >=1.19 gives None, because Go has no operators.
  • PEP 440:
  • >=3.7 gives 3.7.0, ~=3.10 gives 3.10.0, ==3.12.* gives 3.12.0, ==3.12 gives 3.12.0, and >=v3.8 gives 3.8.0.
  • >3.9 gives 3.9.1, and >= 3.8 (with a space) gives 3.8.0.
  • >=3.9,<4 gives 3.9.0, and >=3.8,>=3.10 gives 3.10.0 because the higher bound wins within AND.
  • Invalid in the dialect, so None: ^3.12, ~=3, >=3.*, ===3.12, and >=3.8 || >=3.9.
  • Unbounded, so None: <3.12, !=3.9.*, and the empty string.
  • Poetry:
  • ^3.12 gives 3.12.0, ~3.12 gives 3.12.0, 3.* gives 3.0.0, and >3.9 gives 3.9.1.
  • >=3.8 <4.0 (whitespace AND) gives 3.8.0, and >=3.8,<4.0 (comma AND) gives 3.8.0.
  • ^3.9 || ^3.11 gives 3.9.0, and ^3.11 | ^3.9 gives 3.9.0.
  • * gives None.
  • npm:
  • >=18.0.0 gives 18.0.0, ^20.11.0 gives 20.11.0, ~18.2 gives 18.2.0, 20.x gives 20.0.0, 20 gives 20.0.0, =20.1.0 gives 20.1.0, and v20.1.0 gives 20.1.0.
  • >1 gives 2.0.0, >18.2 gives 18.3.0, and >18.2.3 gives 18.2.4. These match node-semver's minVersion.
  • >=18.17.0 <23 gives 18.17.0, >= 18.17.0 gives 18.17.0, 1.2 - 2.3.4 gives 1.2.0, and 20.0.0-rc.1 gives 20.0.0.
  • ^18.18.0 || ^20.9.0 || >=21.1.0 gives 18.18.0, and so does the same range with its alternatives in reverse order.
  • Unbounded, so None: *, x, "", <16, and ^18 || <16.
  • Any dialect: banana gives None. It doesn't raise.

For compare_language():

  • A bound below block gives BLOCK.
  • A bound between block and warn gives WARN.
  • A bound at or above warn gives OK.
  • A bound exactly equal to block gives WARN, not BLOCK.
  • An unbounded or unparseable declaration gives NOOP, never OK.

tests/unit/languages/test_{go,python,nodejs}.py, for each language class:

  • It skips node_modules.
  • Python:
  • When PEP 621 and Poetry both declare a version, requires-python wins.
  • requires-python uses the PEP440 dialect, and Poetry python uses the POETRY dialect.
  • Go:
  • It ignores the toolchain directive.
  • A go.mod with no go directive produces go 1.16 (implicit).

docs.title: Implementation notes
docs.text:
Where the code differs from the plan above:

  • lower_bound() raises instead of returning None. It raises UngradeableError with a reason ("has no lower bound", "isn't a PEP 440 version specifier", and so on). compare_language() catches it and returns a LanguageGrade{check, lower_bound, reason}, so the reason can be logged with --debug. In the test cases above, "gives None" means "raises UngradeableError".
  • LanguageDeclaration is its own dataclass (version, raw_constraint, dialect) in schemas/language.py, not a wrapper around Package. Nothing in the language path needs Package's specification list.
  • Rubrical.check_all() was added and is what grade calls. It runs check_languages() first, then the unchanged check_package_managers().
  • Report text quotes the declared range, for example requires-python ">=3.7" < v3.10.0. Without the quotes, engines.node >=18.17.0 <23 < v20.0.0 was hard to read.
  • The GitHub reporter escapes | in table cells. Before this, no reported value could contain |, but || ranges would have split the markdown table row.
  • Thresholds are parsed with the same version rules. A warn or block that isn't a version (for example latest) gives NOOP with a reason, rather than failing the run.
  • Language test files are named test_language_*.py in tests/unit/languages/, because the test directories have no __init__.py and test_go.py, test_python.py and test_nodejs.py already exist under tests/unit/package_managers/.
  • The "Dependency" column wasn't renamed. For languages it shows python, go or nodejs, which reads well enough.

docs.title: Related findings
docs.text:
These come from reviewing the comparison code. They are out of scope here, but I don't want new tests to enshrine them:

  • Unparseable versions give OK. In compare_package_semver, ValueError from semver produces OK, so any dependency pinned to a version that isn't full semver (such as 1.19) passes silently. It should probably be NOOP.
  • || ranges are dropped. NodeJS._parse_packagelock skips any dependency whose version contains || without logging it, so those dependencies are never graded.
  • Fixed: whitespace after an operator broke npm parsing. node-semver accepts >= 1.2.3, but NodeJS._parse_packagelock split on spaces first, so >= 1.2.3 was graded as a pinned 1.2.3. The parser now removes whitespace between an operator and its version before parsing.
  • Fixed: bare partial npm versions were graded as exact. In npm, 20 is an X-range (>=20.0.0 <21.0.0-0), but the Node.js package manager mapped it to EQ 20, which semver can't parse, so it got OK. Partial versions and every X-range spelling (1, 1.2, 1.x, 1.x.x, 1.2.*) now map to APPROX_EQ.
  • Still open: leading = and partial versions with <. In npm, =1.2.3 is the same as 1.2.3, but rubrical keeps the = and fails to parse the version, so it gets OK. And <1.2 means <1.2.0-0, but 1.2 can't be parsed as semver, so it also gets OK.

docs.title: Read language version files
docs.text: Status: implemented (2026-10-24). Decisions are recorded in ADR 0004, which builds on ADR 0003 and its plan.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Language checks read only pyproject.toml, go.mod, and package.json. A repository that pins its runtime only in .python-version, .node-version, .nvmrc, or .go-version gets no language result, even though CI (setup-python, setup-node, setup-go) and local tooling use that file to pick the runtime.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• Grade .python-version, .node-version, .nvmrc, and .go-version with the existing languages config, thresholds, and reporting.
  • Read each file the way the tool that owns it reads it, so rubrical doesn't grade content the tool would interpret differently.
  • Keep the ADR 0003 rule that a language check is never silently OK: anything that can't be graded is NOOP with a reason logged under --debug.

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
• .tool-versions, mise.toml, uv's .python-versions, runtime.txt, uv.lock, and Dockerfiles.
  • Resolving aliases (lts/*, node, latest, system) or implementation-prefixed requests (pypy3.10, cpython@3.12) to a version.
  • Reconciling a version file with the manifest in the same directory.

docs.title: Verified file formats
docs.text:
Checked against each tool's source or documentation on 2026-10-24. Sources are listed at the end.

File Tool rules How rubrical reads it .python-version pyenv reads every line, keeps the first word of each, skips blank lines and lines whose first word starts with #, and uses all versions. uv reads every line, trimmed, skips blank lines and lines that start with #, and parses the whole line as a request: a version (3.12), a PEP 440 specifier set (>=3.12,<3.13), a variant (3.13t, 3.13+freethreaded), an implementation (pypy3.10, cpython@3.12, cpython-3.12.3-macos-aarch64-none), or a path or executable name. uv's rules: every trimmed line that is not blank and doesn't start with #. A trailing comment (3.12 # pinned), which pyenv allows and uv doesn't, isn't gradeable. .go-version goenv reads the first word of every line, skips blank lines and lines whose first word starts with #, drops .. and words containing /, and uses all versions. setup-go accepts the file through go-version-file. The first word of every line that is not blank and doesn't start with #. .node-version nodenv reads only the first word of the file, with no comment handling. setup-node accepts the file through node-version-file. The first word of the file. .nvmrc nvm removes # and everything after it on each line, trims each line, and skips blank lines. A line containing = is a reserved key=value pair and is ignored. Exactly one other line must remain, or the file is invalid. Aliases such as lts/*, lts/iron, node, and stable are allowed. nvm's rules. If more than one version line remains, the lines are kept together as one value, which isn't gradeable.

docs.title: 1. Dialects
docs.text:
Add two values to VersionDialect and register them in DIALECTS in comparisons/lower_bound.py.

Dialect Used by Alternatives Comparator VERSION_FILE .node-version, .nvmrc, .go-version One per line. A bare version: an optional v, release numbers, and an optional pre-release suffix. An operator, wildcard, or anything else raises UngradeableError. PYTHON_VERSION_FILE .python-version One per line. A line that starts with an operator is split into PEP 440 comparators. A bare version, as above, or a PEP 440 comparator.

Each line is an alternative, so the existing lower_bound() loop gives the lowest version across lines, and one ungradeable line makes the whole file NOOP. Bare versions are padded and suffixes are dropped as in ADR 0003, so 3.13t grades as 3.13.0 and v18.17.1 as 18.17.1.

docs.title: 2. Reading files
docs.text:
Add rubrical/languages/version_files.py with one function per file format, each returning the version lines (an empty list means the file declares nothing). The language classes add the file names to target_files and dispatch on file_details.path.name in parse_file. A file whose function returns no lines returns None, so it produces no result.

raw_constraint is the file name followed by each line quoted, for example .python-version "3.12" "3.11", and version is the lines joined by newlines.

docs.title: 3. Observability
docs.text: Rubrical.check_languages() already logs each declaration, its lower bound, and the NOOP reason under --debug, so no new logging is needed. The UngradeableError reasons name the offending line, for example \`pypy3.10\` is not a version.
